For each integer $n\ge0$, define the Legendre polynomial
$$
P_n(x):=\frac{1}{2^n n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2-1)^n,
$$
with $n!$ as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and repeated derivatives as in [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Define the unweighted pairing of real polynomials by
$$
\langle p,q\rangle_L:=\int_{-1}^1p(x)q(x)\,dx,\qquad \|p\|_L^2:=\langle p,p\rangle_L.
$$
The integral is the ordinary integral of a continuous function; polynomial products are continuous and hence integrable by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. The normalization and all polynomial identities needed for the orthogonal Galerkin scale are proved in [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]].

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]), and suppose

$$f(a) \;=\; f(b) .$$

Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.

**Three hypotheses, three different jobs.** Continuity on the **closed**
interval is what the extreme value theorem consumes; differentiability on the
**open** interval is what Fermat's theorem consumes, and it is asked for
nowhere else; and $f(a) = f(b)$ is what forces the extremum inside when neither
extremum is attained in the interior. Continuity at the two endpoints cannot be
dropped, and a false statement later on this page records a witness for that.

**Differentiability is meant with respect to the domain $[a,b]$.** For $c$ in
the open interval that is the same condition as differentiability of any
restriction of $f$ to a subinterval around $c$, since only points near $c$
enter, but the phrase is fixed here so that the citation of
[[thm-fermat-interior-extremum]], whose hypothesis is interiority in the
domain, is exact.

derivations.claim: Suppose $P_p$ has only $m<p$ sign-changing roots $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ in $(-1,1)$ and set $q(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m(x-r_j)$, with $q=1$ if $m=0$. At each sign-changing root both $P_p$ and $q$ change sign, while at every other real root $P_p$ does not change sign; therefore $P_pq$ has one constant sign on $(-1,1)$ and is not identically zero. It is continuous and nonzero on some open interval, so its integral is nonzero. But $\deg q=m<p$, and [F2] gives $\int_{-1}^1P_pq=0$, a contradiction. Thus $P_p$ has at least $p$ sign-changing roots in the open interval.

A degree-$p$ polynomial cannot have more than $p$ distinct roots. The $p$ roots obtained in step 1.1 therefore exhaust its degree; each has multiplicity one and there are no other roots. Rolle's theorem [F3] between consecutive roots gives $p-1$ distinct roots of $P_p'$ in $(-1,1)$. Since $P_p'$ has degree $p-1$, these are all its roots and each is simple. None equals an endpoint, so adjoining $-1$ and $1$ gives $p+1$ distinct nodes, including the case $p=1$ where there are no interior critical points.

derivations.claim: Apply Leibniz's rule to the $n$th derivative in the definition. Every term differentiates $(1-t)^{n+d-1}$ at most $n$ times, so it contains a factor $(1-t)^{d-1}$. After division the result is a polynomial. The original factor has degree $2n+d-1$ and leading coefficient $(-1)^{n+d-1}$; differentiating $n$ times and dividing by the leading term $(-1)^{d-1}t^{d-1}$ of $(1-t)^{d-1}$ shows that $\phi_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\binom{2n+d-1}{n}$. The coefficient of $t^n$ in $t^n(1-t)^{n+d-1}$ is $1$, so its $n$th derivative at zero is $n!$ and $\phi_n(0)=(-1)^n$.

If $r$ has degree below $n$, multiply the Rodrigues formula by $w_dr$ and integrate. Integrating by parts $n$ times is allowed by [A1] and gives $\int_0^1w_d(t)\phi_n(t)r(t)\,dt=\frac1{n!}\int_0^1t^n(1-t)^{n+d-1}r^{(n)}(t)\,dt=0$, because $r^{(n)}=0$. Thus $\phi_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial, and the degree conclusion in step 1.1 makes the family an orthogonal basis of each polynomial space.

For nonnegative integers $a,b$, let $B(a,b)=\int_0^1t^a(1-t)^b\,dt$. The case $a=0$ gives $B(0,b)=1/(b+1)$; for $a\ge1$, integration by parts with $u=t^a$ and $dv=(1-t)^b\,dt$ gives $B(a,b)=aB(a-1,b+1)/(b+1)$. Iterating yields $B(a,b)=a!b!/(a+b+1)!$. Applying $n$ integrations by parts to the Rodrigues formula with $r(t)=t^n$ gives $\int_0^1w_d\phi_nt^n\,dt=B(n,n+d-1)=n!(n+d-1)!/(2n+d)!$. Since $t^n=\phi_n/\kappa_n+r$ for some $r$ of degree below $n$, where $\kappa_n=\binom{2n+d-1}{n}$, orthogonality gives $\|\phi_n\|_{L^2(w_d)}^2=\kappa_n B(n,n+d-1)=1/(2n+d)$.

Write $q=\sum_{n=0}^pc_n\phi_n$. By the endpoint and norm identities, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|q(0)|^2=\left|\sum_{n=0}^pc_n(-1)^n\right|^2\le\left(\sum_{n=0}^p(2n+d)\right)\left(\sum_{n=0}^p\frac{|c_n|^2}{2n+d}\right)=(p+1)(p+d)\|q\|_{L^2(w_d)}^2$. Equality is attained by the polynomial $K_p(t,0)=\sum_{n=0}^p(2n+d)(-1)^n\phi_n(t)$: its endpoint value and squared norm both equal $\sum_{n=0}^p(2n+d)=(p+1)(p+d)$. Hence the evaluation norm squared is exactly the stated value.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

derivations.claim: Since $\omega_\alpha>0$ in the interior, a nonzero polynomial cannot have weighted square integral zero: continuity gives a ball on which its absolute value is bounded below by a positive number. Integrability follows from $\alpha_j\ge0$ on the bounded simplex. Hence the weighted inner product is positive definite on each finite-dimensional polynomial space. Orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb P_{n-1}$ therefore gives the finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition $\mathbb P_n=E_0\oplus\cdots\oplus E_n$. The scale in the Statement is the completion of this orthogonal-sum norm, so its coefficient description and truncation are well-defined.

For a finite sum $u=\sum u_n$, orthogonality gives $\|u-P_pu\|_{\mathcal H_\alpha^\ell}^2=\sum_{n>p}(1+\mu_n)^\ell\|u_n\|_\alpha^2\le(1+\mu_{p+1})^{\ell-m}\sum_{n>p}(1+\mu_n)^m\|u_n\|_\alpha^2$, because $\mu_n=n(n+d+|\alpha|)$ is increasing for $n\ge0$. Taking square roots proves the tail estimate for finite sums.

Truncation is contractive in every coefficient norm $\mathcal H_\alpha^s$, and finite sums are dense by the definition of the completion. The finite-sum estimate in step 2.1 therefore passes to every $u\in\mathcal H_\alpha^m$. If $q\in\mathbb P_p$, each degree layer has $n\le p$, so $(1+\mu_n)^{m-\ell}\le(1+\mu_p)^{m-\ell}$ term by term; summing proves the inverse estimate. Neither argument invokes a derivative norm, which is why neither implies an unweighted Sobolev estimate.

Let $d\ge2$ and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. A **degree map** is a function $p:\mathcal T\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite values. The broken simplex space associated with $(\mathcal T,p)$ is
$$
V^{\mathrm{br}}(\mathcal T,p):=\{v\in L^2(\Omega):v|_K\in\mathbb P_{p_K}(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\},
$$
where $p_K:=p(K)$ and $\mathbb P_m(K)$ denotes restrictions of real polynomials of total degree at most $m$. Its **conforming hp space** is the subspace of functions whose two polynomial traces agree on every interior facet. The zero-boundary hp space further requires the polynomial trace to vanish on every boundary facet. For an interior facet $F=K\cap K'$, its trace degree is $p_F:=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; equality of the two traces means that their common polynomial belongs to $\mathbb P_{p_F}(F)$.

A **matching affine tensor-box mesh** is a finite face-to-face partition of a bounded polytope into affine images of $[-1,1]^d$, with pairwise disjoint interiors. For a scalar degree $p_K$ on each box, the local tensor space is $\mathbb Q_{p_K}(K)$, the pullback of polynomials of degree at most $p_K$ in each reference coordinate. The conforming box hp space is defined by equality of polynomial traces across every shared face, and its zero-boundary subspace by zero traces on the exterior faces. For a shared face $F=K\cap K'$, set $p_F=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; its common trace lies in $\mathbb Q_{p_F}(F)$ in tangential reference coordinates. This definition of tensor boxes does not include curved or non-affine cells.

On either mesh, **h-refinement** replaces one cell by a finite matching partition of that cell and assigns degrees to the children; **p-refinement** raises at least one cell degree while leaving the mesh fixed; **hp-refinement** performs both operations. A local polynomial basis is **hierarchical** if its ordered degree layers span the nested spaces $\mathbb P_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb P_p$ (or $\mathbb Q_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb Q_p$), with each new layer extending the preceding span. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$

[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$

$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$

axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

This holds for every coordinate $i$, and step 1.1 supplies $v,g_i\in L^2$; hence $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ with the stated cellwise weak gradient. Together with the simplex branch of step 1.1 this proves the assertion for both mesh types.

For $p\ge1$ and $g\in L^2(-1,1)$, define the degree-$(p-1)$ Legendre orthogonal projection
$$
\Pi_{p-1}g:=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}\frac{2n+1}{2}\left(\int_{-1}^1g(t)P_n(t)\,dt\right)P_n.
$$
For $c\in\mathbb R$, define the endpoint-anchored integrated projector
$$
\mathcal I_p(c,g)(x):=c+\int_{-1}^x\Pi_{p-1}g(t)\,dt,\qquad -1\le x\le1.
$$
If an absolutely continuous function $f$ is represented as $f(x)=f(-1)+\int_{-1}^xf'(t)\,dt$ with $f'\in L^2$, write $I_pf:=\mathcal I_p(f(-1),f')$. The finite sum and integral are defined for every such input; no choice axiom is used in this definition.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.

For $s\ge0$, define $H_L^s$ as the completion of finite Legendre sums $p=\sum_{n=0}^Mc_nP_n$ in the coefficient norm
$$
\|p\|_{H_L^s}^2=\sum_{n=0}^M(1+n(n+1))^s\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2.
$$
The coefficients are unique because the polynomials have distinct degrees by [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]]. At $s=0$ this norm is exactly the unweighted $L^2([-1,1])$ norm on finite sums, by the same lemma; its completion is denoted $L_L^2$. Define the degree-$N$ orthogonal projection on finite sums by
$$
\Pi_Nu=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_nP_n.
$$
It extends to the coefficient completion by truncation. This explicitly coefficient-defined scale uses the Legendre weight $1$ on $[-1,1]$; no equivalence with an unweighted derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted here.

For fixed $s\ge0$, $x\mapsto x^s$ is nondecreasing on $(0,\infty)$: its derivative is $s x^{s-1}\ge0$ by [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] and real powers are positive by [[def-real-power]] and [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], so the mean-value theorem [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] applies. $$\left\{(c_n)_{n\ge0}:\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n(n+1))^s\frac{2}{2n+1}|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Finite-support sequences are dense by truncation, and completeness of $\ell^2$ from [[lem-square-summable-sequences-form-a-hilbert-space]] makes this the completion.

$$

$$

$$

Its **conforming hp space** is the subspace of functions whose two polynomial traces agree on every interior facet. The zero-boundary hp space further requires the polynomial trace to vanish on every boundary facet. For an interior facet $F=K\cap K'$, its trace degree is $p_F:=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; equality of the two traces means that their common polynomial belongs to $\mathbb P_{p_F}(F)$.

A **matching affine tensor-box mesh** is a finite face-to-face partition of a bounded polytope into affine images of $[-1,1]^d$, with pairwise disjoint interiors. For a scalar degree $p_K$ on each box, the local tensor space is $\mathbb Q_{p_K}(K)$, the pullback of polynomials of degree at most $p_K$ in each reference coordinate. The conforming box hp space is defined by equality of polynomial traces across every shared face, and its zero-boundary subspace by zero traces on the exterior faces. For a shared face $F=K\cap K'$, set $p_F=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; its common trace lies in $\mathbb Q_{p_F}(F)$ in tangential reference coordinates. This definition of tensor boxes does not include curved or non-affine cells.

On either mesh, **h-refinement** replaces one cell by a finite matching partition of that cell and assigns degrees to the children; **p-refinement** raises at least one cell degree while leaving the mesh fixed; **hp-refinement** performs both operations. The quotient extends to a polynomial of degree $n$. These polynomials are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(w_d\,dt)$, with
$$\phi_n(0)=(-1)^n,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(\phi_n)=\binom{2n+d-1}{n},\qquad \int_0^1w_d\phi_n^2\,dt=\frac1{2n+d}.$$

Let $d\ge2$ and let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of a bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. A **degree map** is a function $p:\mathcal T\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite values. The broken simplex space associated with $(\mathcal T,p)$ is
$$
V^{\mathrm{br}}(\mathcal T,p):=\{v\in L^2(\Omega):v|_K\in\mathbb P_{p_K}(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\},
$$
where $p_K:=p(K)$ and $\mathbb P_m(K)$ denotes restrictions of real polynomials of total degree at most $m$. Its **conforming hp space** is the subspace of functions whose two polynomial traces agree on every interior facet. The zero-boundary hp space further requires the polynomial trace to vanish on every boundary facet. For an interior facet $F=K\cap K'$, its trace degree is $p_F:=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; equality of the two traces means that their common polynomial belongs to $\mathbb P_{p_F}(F)$.

A **matching affine tensor-box mesh** is a finite face-to-face partition of a bounded polytope into affine images of $[-1,1]^d$, with pairwise disjoint interiors. For a scalar degree $p_K$ on each box, the local tensor space is $\mathbb Q_{p_K}(K)$, the pullback of polynomials of degree at most $p_K$ in each reference coordinate. The conforming box hp space is defined by equality of polynomial traces across every shared face, and its zero-boundary subspace by zero traces on the exterior faces. For a shared face $F=K\cap K'$, set $p_F=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$; its common trace lies in $\mathbb Q_{p_F}(F)$ in tangential reference coordinates. This definition of tensor boxes does not include curved or non-affine cells.

On either mesh, **h-refinement** replaces one cell by a finite matching partition of that cell and assigns degrees to the children; **p-refinement** raises at least one cell degree while leaving the mesh fixed; **hp-refinement** performs both operations. A local polynomial basis is **hierarchical** if its ordered degree layers span the nested spaces $\mathbb P_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb P_p$ (or $\mathbb Q_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathbb Q_p$), with each new layer extending the preceding span. For example, pullbacks of reference monomials $\widehat x^\nu$ ordered by $|\nu|$ give such a basis for $\mathbb P_p$, and tensor monomials $\xi^\nu$ ordered by $\max_i\nu_i$ give one for $\mathbb Q_p$. This basis convention does not assert stability of a particular basis or projector.

Let $(\mathcal T_k)_{k\ge1}$ be nested finite matching shape-regular affine triangulations of $\Omega$, with at most $C_0k$ triangles. Write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(T,\mathcal C)=\inf_{x\in T,c\in\mathcal C}|x-c|$. Assume a fixed $0<\sigma<1$ and $C_1>0$ satisfy

Let $p_k\in\mathbb N$ be uniform total polynomial degrees with $c_0k\le p_k\le c_1k$ for fixed $0<c_0\le c_1$. For a fixed union $\Gamma_D$ of polygon edges, let $V_k$ be the space of broken piecewise-$\mathbb P_{p_k}$ functions whose polynomial traces agree on every interior edge and vanish on the boundary edges in $\Gamma_D$; put $N_k=\dim V_k$. This is the corresponding subspace of the variable-degree space in [[def-hp-variable-degree-spaces-on-matching-meshes]].
For this smoother class, the boundary condition means that the unique continuous representative supplied by [[lem-hp-weighted-analytic-corner-pointwise-control]] vanishes pointwise on the edges in $\Gamma_D$; no zero condition is imposed on the other edges. If $u\in B^2_\beta(\Omega)$ satisfies this boundary condition, then constants $C,b>0$, independent of $k$, satisfy

$$
\inf_{v_k\in V_k}\|\nabla(u-v_k)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le Ce^{-bN_k^{1/3}}.
$$

For a bounded coercive conforming Galerkin problem on a Hilbert space $V\subset H^1(\Omega)$ containing $u$, with $V_k\subset V$ and norm equivalent to the gradient seminorm on $V$, Céa's estimate gives the same exponential rate for the energy error, with its actual $M/\alpha$ and norm-equivalence factors included. The constants may depend on the polygon, weights, weighted analytic bounds, mesh shape and grading constants, degree constants, $\Gamma_D$, and the Galerkin coercivity and norm-equivalence constants.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded open polygonal domain with finitely many straight sides and corner set $\mathcal C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_m\}$, with interior angle at each corner strictly between $0$ and $2\pi$. Let $0\le\beta_i<1$ and write $\Phi_\gamma(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m|x-c_i|^{\gamma_i}$ for a vector $\gamma\in[0,\infty)^m$. For integer $k\ge2$, define

$$
\|v\|_{H^{k,2}_\beta(\Omega)}^2=\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{j=2}^k\sum_{|\alpha|=j}\|\Phi_{\beta+j-2}D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2,

where $(\beta+j-2)_i=\beta_i+j-2$ and a zero exponent contributes the factor one. Let $u\in H^{k,2}_\beta(\Omega)$ for every integer $k\ge2$, with real-valued weak derivatives, and suppose constants $C_u,d_u>0$ satisfy

\left\|\Phi_{\beta+j-2}\sum_{|\alpha|=j}|D^\alpha u|\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_ud_u^{j-2}(j-2)!\qquad(j\ge2).

For each fixed $0<a<\min_i(1-\beta_i)$ there are constants $C,A,R>0$ such that the weak class of $u$ has a unique representative $\widetilde u\in C(\overline\Omega)$, smooth up to every open side away from corners, and for $0<r=|x-c_i|<R$,

$$

$$

On every compact subset of $\overline\Omega\setminus\mathcal C$, the derivatives satisfy ordinary factorial bounds $|D^\alpha u|\le C_0A_0^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$. derivations.claim: With $\lambda=2/3$, polar differentiation gives $|u|=r^\lambda|\sin(\lambda\theta)|$ and $|\nabla u|^2=\lambda^2r^{2\lambda-2}$. The origin is on the boundary and $u$ is smooth in $\Omega$, so these classical derivatives are its weak derivatives; hence $u\in H^1(\Omega)$.

In the polar orthonormal frame the Hessian entries are $u_{rr}=\lambda(\lambda-1)r^{\lambda-2}\sin(\lambda\theta)$, $u_{r\theta}^{\rm orth}=\lambda(\lambda-1)r^{\lambda-2}\cos(\lambda\theta)$, and $u_{\theta\theta}^{\rm orth}=\lambda(1-\lambda)r^{\lambda-2}\sin(\lambda\theta)$. Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Since $q(0)=0$, polynomial division gives a polynomial $R$ of degree at most $p-1$ when $p\ge1$; for $p=0$ or $p=1$ the endpoint conditions force $q=0$. Thus $Lq$ has total degree at most $p$. At $y=0$, $R(1)=q(1)=0$, so $Lq=q(x)$; at $x=0$ it is zero; and on $x+y=1$ one has $1-y=x$, so $xR(1-y)=xR(x)=q(x)$.

Put $A=\int_0^1|q'(t)|^2dt$. Polynomial integration term by term gives $q(t)=\int_0^tq'(s)ds$, so Cauchy–Schwarz [F3] yields $t|R(t)|^2\le\int_0^t|q'(s)|^2ds\le A$ and hence $\int_0^1t|R(t)|^2dt\le A$. The identity $tR'(t)=q'(t)-R(t)$ gives $\int_0^1t^3|R'(t)|^2dt\le2\int_0^1t|q'|^2+2\int_0^1t|R|^2\le4A$. Also $|q(t)|^2\le tA$, so $\int_0^1|q|^2\le A$. Writing $t=1-y$, the slices of $T$ are $0<x<t$. Therefore $\|\partial_xLq\|_2^2\le2\int_0^1(1-x)|q'(x)|^2dx+2\int_0^1t|R(t)|^2dt\le4A,$ $\|\partial_yLq\|_2^2=\frac13\int_0^1t^3|R'(t)|^2dt\le\frac43A,$ and $\|Lq\|_2^2\le2\int_0^1(1-x)|q(x)|^2dx+\frac23\int_0^1t^3|R(t)|^2dt\le\frac83A.$ Fubini [F3] justifies the slice integrals. Using the Sobolev norm definition [F2], adding the three inequalities gives $\|Lq\|_{H^1(T)}^2\le8A\le16A$, proving the safe constant four.

Lift the three residuals separately by step 1.1; each lift vanishes on the other two edges. Their sum plus $a$ therefore has trace exactly $g$ and degree at most $p$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $m,n\ge0$, the polynomials of [[def-legendre-polynomial-family-and-l2-pairing]] satisfy
$$\int_{-1}^1P_n(x)P_m(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn}, \qquad \int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'(x)P_m'(x)\,dx=\frac{2n(n+1)}{2n+1}\,\delta_{mn},$$
where $\delta_{mn}=1$ if $m=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $P_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient, so $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ form a basis of polynomials of degree at most $N$.
For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on

derivations.claim: Fix $k\ge1$ and put $w_k(x)=(1-x^2)^k$. For $n\ge k$, the polynomial $Q_{n,k}:=D^k(w_kD^kP_n)$ has degree $n$. Integrating by parts $k$ times moves the outer derivative block onto a polynomial $q$ and gives $\int Q_{n,k}q=(-1)^k\int w_kD^kP_nD^kq=\int P_nD^k(w_kD^kq)$; all boundary terms vanish because derivatives of $w_k$ of orders below $k$ vanish at both endpoints. The final polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree at most $\deg q<n$, so [F1] makes the integral zero. The leading coefficient of $Q_{n,k}$ is $(-1)^k(n+k)!/(n-k)!$ times the leading coefficient of $P_n$. Orthogonality and the degree statement in [F1] therefore give $Q_{n,k}=(-1)^k\lambda_{n,k}P_n$, where $\lambda_{n,k}=(n+k)!/(n-k)!$.

For $n,m\ge k$, integrate by parts $k$ times and use step 1.1 to obtain $\int_{-1}^1w_kP_n^{(k)}P_m^{(k)}=(-1)^k\int_{-1}^1P_nD^k(w_kP_m^{(k)})=\lambda_{m,k}\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first identity in [F1] makes this zero for $n\ne m$ and equal to $\lambda_{n,k}2/(2n+1)$ for $n=m$, proving the repeated derivative orthogonality formula.

Write $c_n=(f,P_n)_{L^2}/\|P_n\|_2^2$. The absolutely continuous representatives in [F3] justify $k$ integrations by parts; all boundary terms vanish because $w_k$ has endpoint zeros of order $k$. Step 1.1 then gives $\int_{-1}^1w_kf^{(k)}P_n^{(k)}=\lambda_{n,k}c_n\|P_n\|_2^2\qquad(n\ge k).$ The functions $w_k^{1/2}P_n^{(k)}$ are mutually orthogonal by step 2.1 and have squared norms $\lambda_{n,k}\|P_n\|_2^2$. Density [F2] and the best-approximation property of finite orthogonal projections imply $\Pi_Mf\to f$ in $L^2$: first approximate $f$ by a polynomial and then take $M$ at least its degree. Orthogonality [F1] and Pythagoras give $\|f-\Pi_Nf\|_2^2=\sum_{n>N}|c_n|^2\|P_n\|_2^2$. Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: For $0<\tau<1$ and integer $n\ge1$ define $B_{n,\tau}(t)=\sum_{j=\lceil n\tau\rceil}^n\binom njt^j(1-t)^{n-j}$. Then $0\le B\le1$, $\deg B\le n$, and $|B'|\le n$. If $t\le\tau-\delta$ for fixed $\delta>0$, Chernoff's bound follows directly from $1_{j\ge n\tau}\le e^{z(j-n\tau)}$ for $z>0$: $B_{n,\tau}(t)\le e^{-zn\tau}(1-t+te^z)^n.$ For sufficiently small fixed $z$, the exponent per $n$ is negative uniformly because its derivative at $z=0$ is $t-\tau\le-\delta$. Applying the same argument to the complementary lower tail gives exponential smallness of $1-B$ on $t\ge\tau+\delta$. Differentiation telescopes to one binomial atom times $n$; away from the threshold its probability is bounded by the same tail estimate with gap $\delta/2$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and increasing the constant covers the finitely many smaller $n$. Thus $B$ and $1-B$ switch from exponentially small to $1+O(e^{-cn})$ across a strip of fixed width, and their derivatives outside that strip are $O(ne^{-cn})$.

Choose $0<\rho<1/(32A)$ and a finite coordinate-grid cover of $S$ by boxes of radius $\rho$ with centers $a_i\in S$, $1\le i\le m$. In each coordinate form a left increasing binomial factor with threshold $a_{i,j}-3\rho/2$ and a right decreasing factor with threshold $a_{i,j}+3\rho/2$; omit the left factor when its threshold is at most zero and the right factor when its threshold is at least one. Their product $b_i$ has degree at most $4n$, lies in $[0,1]$, equals $1+O(e^{-cn})$ on the inner box of radius $\rho$ and its first derivatives there are $O(ne^{-cn})$; outside the outer box of radius $2\rho$ its value and first derivatives are $O(ne^{-cn})$. The omitted boundary factors require no suppression on a side where the outer box does not meet $S$.

Let $T_{i,s}$ be the total-degree-$s$ Taylor polynomial at $a_i$. When $a_i$ is on the boundary, take limits of interior centers; all derivatives extend continuously to $S$. On the intersection of the outer box and $S$, convexity keeps the Taylor segment inside the triangle, so [F1] and the multinomial formula give $|f-T_{i,s}|+|\nabla(f-T_{i,s})|\le CM(s+1)(4A\rho)^s\le CM2^{-s}$ after enlarging $C$ for small $s$. On all of $S$, the coefficient formula for $T_{i,s}$ gives $|T_{i,s}|+|\nabla T_{i,s}|\le CM(s+1)^2D^s$ for a fixed $D>1$ depending only on $A$.

Set $w_i=b_i\prod_{j<i}(1-b_j)$ and $w_0=\prod_{j\le m}(1-b_j)$. Then $\sum_{i=0}^m w_i=1$ and $0\le w_i\le1$. At every point of $S$ some inner box applies, so one factor $1-b_i$, together with its first derivatives, is exponentially small there; the product rule and $|b_j'|\le Cn$ give $\|w_0\|_{W^{1,\infty}(S)}\le Cne^{-cn}$. Outside the outer box for a fixed $i$, the same product rule gives $|w_i|+|\nabla w_i|\le Cne^{-cn}$.

Put $q=\sum_{i=1}^m w_iT_{i,s}$. Since $f-q=w_0f+\sum_iw_i(f-T_{i,s})$, the near-box and far-box bounds of steps 3.1 and 3.2 give $\|f-q\|_{W^{1,\infty}(S)}\le CM\{n2^{-s}+n(s+1)^2D^se^{-cn}\}.$ Choose fixed $\varepsilon>0$ with $\varepsilon\le1$ and $\varepsilon\log D<c/2$, and let $s=\lfloor\varepsilon n\rfloor$. Then the right side is at most $CM e^{-b_0n}$. Each $w_i$ has degree at most $4mn$, so $q$ has total degree at most $4mn+s\le(4m+1)n$. Choose $n=\lfloor p/(4m+1)\rfloor$; for the finitely many $p$ with $n=0$, the zero polynomial and an enlarged constant handle the claim. This proves the exponential estimate for every $p\ge1$.

On the interval let $P$ be the $L^2$ orthogonal projection of $f'$ onto $\mathbb P_{p-1}$ and put $J_pf(t)=f(0)+\int_0^tP(s)ds$. The positive-definite finite polynomial Gram matrix gives a unique projection; Pythagoras gives $\|P\|_2\le\|f'\|_2$ and $\|f'-P\|_2\le\|f'-r\|_2$ for every $r\in\mathbb P_{p-1}$. Orthogonality to constants gives $\int_0^1P=\int_0^1f'$, and [F4] evaluates the latter as $f(1)-f(0)$. Thus $J_pf(1)=f(0)+\int_0^1P=f(1)$, while $J_pf(0)=f(0)$ by construction. The derivatives of $f'$ satisfy a factorial bound with fixed constants $M'=MA$ and $A'=2A$, since $(j+1)!\le2^j j!$ for $j\ge1$. For $p\ge2$, apply step 4.1 to $f'$ with degree $p-1$; best approximation of the $L^2$ projection then gives $\|f'-P\|_2\le CMe^{-b(p-1)}$, which is at most $C'Me^{-b'p}$ after changing constants. For $p=1$, the derivative contraction and the bound $\|f'\|_2\le MA$ give the same asserted estimate after enlarging $C'$. Finally $f-J_pf=\int_0^t(f'-P)$ and [F2] bounds its $L^2$ norm by $\|f'-P\|_2$. The derivative and value bounds prove the stated interval estimate.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The coefficients satisfy $3-2=1$ for values and $-3+4=1$ for first normal derivatives. For a smooth test $\phi$ across $x=0$, changing variables in the zeroth-order pairing gives $\psi_0(t)=\phi(t)-3\phi(-t)+2\phi(-t/2)$, so $\psi_0(0)=0$. For the first normal derivative, the corresponding test combination is $\psi_1(t)=\phi(t)+3\phi(-t)-4\phi(-t/2)$, also with $\psi_1(0)=0$. These formulas follow by rewriting the reflected integrals over $t>0$ and applying the chain rule. Multiply each combined test by a cutoff that is zero on $(0,\varepsilon)$ and one on $(2\varepsilon,\infty)$ before using the weak derivative identity on the original open square. If $|\chi_\varepsilon\prime|\le C/\varepsilon$, then $|\psi_j\chi_\varepsilon\prime|\le C$ on the strip because $\psi_j(t)=O(t)$; for any relevant $g\in L^2$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the cutoff error by $C\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\|g\|_{L^2(0,2\varepsilon)}\le C\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\|g\|_{L^2(0,1)}\to0$. Thus the reflected piecewise formulas are the weak derivatives through order two, including mixed derivatives. Changes of variables bound each derivative norm by a fixed multiple of $\|v\|_{H^2}$. Reflect successively across the four sides, cut off in the enlarged square, and mollify. For every weak derivative through order two, inserting a translated compactly supported kernel into its weak derivative identity gives $D^\alpha(v*\varphi_\varepsilon)=(D^\alpha v)*\varphi_\varepsilon$ on the original square: the sign from integration by parts cancels the sign from differentiating the kernel in its integration variable. Thus [F3] gives smooth approximants converging in $H^2$. The smooth inequality makes them uniformly Cauchy, yielding a continuous representative and the same bound for every $H^2$ class. Scaling gives $\|v\|_{L^\infty(Q)}\le C(r^{-1}\|v\|_2+\|Dv\|_2+r\|D^2v\|_2)$ on a rectangle of side comparable to $r$; a parallelogram with fixed aspect ratio has the same estimate after an affine change of variables.

A finite angular cover gives aspect ratios and widths bounded in terms of the fixed corner angles. For each individual weak derivative $g_\alpha=D^\alpha u$ with $|\alpha|=j\ge2$, the weighted hypotheses imply $g_\alpha\in H^2$ on this rectangle. In particular, the coefficients $3,-2$ are not used to extend $u$ in arbitrary Sobolev orders and then differentiated across a reflecting side. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the $k\ge1$ branch. Let $P_n$ be the real Legendre polynomial normalized by $P_n(1)=1$, and let $\Pi_N$ be the $L^2(-1,1;\mathbb R)$ orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb P_N(-1,1)$. For every integer $k\ge1$, every integer $N\ge k-1$, and every real-valued $f\in H^k(-1,1)$,

$$
\|f-\Pi_Nf\|_{L^2(-1,1)}\le\left(\frac{(N+1-k)!}{(N+1+k)!}\right)^{1/2}\|f^{(k)}\|_{L^2(-1,1)}.
$$

For $k=0$, every integer $N\ge0$, and $f\in L^2(-1,1)$, $\|f-\Pi_Nf\|_2\le\|f\|_2$. For $n,m\ge k$ the repeated derivative orthogonality identity is

$$
\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^kP_n^{(k)}(x)P_m^{(k)}(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2n+1}\frac{(n+k)!}{(n-k)!}\,\delta_{nm}.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$. For every integer $k\ge0$ and
$1\le p\le\infty$, there is a bounded linear operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^d)$$
whose restriction to $\widehat S_d$ is the input class. Consequently
$\widehat S_d$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension domain in the sense of
[[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]. The operator may
be chosen with support in one fixed bounded set.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1\le p<\infty$, integer $r\ge1$,
integer $s\ge0$, and real-valued $v\in W^{\max(r,s),p}(\widehat S_d)$.
There is a polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_{r-1}(\widehat S_d)$, chosen by
matching all means $\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha q=
\int_{\widehat S_d}D^\alpha v$ for $|\alpha|\le r-1$, such that:

- if $0\le s\le r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le C|v|_{W^{r,p}(\widehat S_d)}$;
- if $s>r$, then
  $\|v-q\|_{W^{s,p}(\widehat S_d)}\le
  C\sum_{j=r}^{s}|v|_{W^{j,p}(\widehat S_d)}$.

The second clause assumes $v\in W^{s,p}$; constants depend only on
$d,p,r,s$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let
$W\subseteq V$ be a normed subspace over that same field: use [[def-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-normed-subspace]] for $\mathbb C$. If $W$ admits an ordered basis of finite
length, including length zero, then $W$ is closed in $V$. This holds in ZF,
without a choice axiom; the ambient space need not be complete.

derivations.claim: On $I=(-1,1)$ define $S_nf(x)=f(-1)+(x+1)f'(-1)+\int_{-1}^x(x-t)\Pi_{n-2}f''(t)\,dt,$ where $\Pi_{n-2}$ is the ordinary Legendre $L^2$ projection. Here $p\ge2r-4$ implies $n\ge r-2\ge3$. For $f\in H^2(I)$, the endpoint values are those of its absolutely continuous representatives from [F4]. The polynomial $S_nf$ has degree at most $n$ and matches $f,f'$ at $-1$. Its second derivative is an $L^2$ contraction; integrating twice and using the one-dimensional endpoint estimate gives $\|S_nf\|_{H^2(I)}\le C\|f\|_{H^2(I)}$ with absolute $C$. For every integer $s\ge3$ with $n\ge s-1$, the error $e=f-S_nf$ has $e(-1)=e'(-1)=0$ and $e''=f''-\Pi_{n-2}f''$. Apply the Legendre tail estimate to $f''$ with derivative order $s-2$ and projection degree $n-2$; the factorial ratio is $\rho_{n,s}=\left(\frac{(n-s+1)!}{(n+s-3)!}\right)^{1/2}.$ Two integrations of $e''$, with Cauchy–Schwarz [F5], give $\|e\|_{H^2(I)}\le C\rho_{n,s}\|f^{(s)}\|_2$. The same inequality holds for each derivative of order at most two.

Put $\mathbb Q_n=\operatorname{span}\{x^iy^j:0\le i,j\le n\}$, apply $S_n$ in each coordinate on $I^2$, and write $S_n^x,S_n^y$. For smooth $U$, $U-S_n^xS_n^yU=(1-S_n^x)U+S_n^x(1-S_n^y)U.$ Let $a+b\le2$. For the first term choose $s_b=r-\max(1,b)$, so $s_b\in\{r-1,r-2\}$, $s_b\ge3$, $n\ge s_b-1$, and $s_b+b\le r$. Step 1.1 on the $x$ sections of $D_y^bU$ bounds $\|D_x^aD_y^b(1-S_n^x)U\|_2$ by $C\rho_{n,s_b}\|D_x^{s_b}D_y^bU\|_2$. For the second term, the uniform $H^2_x$ bound in step 1.1 bounds its $D_x^aD_y^b$ norm by $C\sum_{j=0}^2\|D_x^jD_y^b(1-S_n^y)U\|_2$. For each such $j$, choose $t_j=r-\max(1,j)\in\{r-1,r-2\}$; then $t_j\ge3$, $n\ge t_j-1$, and $j+t_j\le r$. Apply the $H^2_y$ error estimate of step 1.1 to $D_x^jU$; it bounds every $y$ derivative of order $b\le2$ in this sum by $C\rho_{n,t_j}\|D_x^jD_y^{t_j}U\|_2$. Because $\rho_{n,r-1}\le\rho_{n,r-2}=\eta_{n,r}$, all terms are bounded by $C\eta_{n,r}\|U\|_{H^r(I^2)}$. Fubini [F5] and addition over $a+b\le2$ give $\|U-S_n^xS_n^yU\|_{H^2(I^2)}\le C\eta_{n,r}\|U\|_{H^r(I^2)}.$ For the inputs used below, namely restrictions of $H^r(\mathbb R^2)$ extensions, choose smooth whole-space approximants by [F4]. The estimate on their differences makes $S_n^xS_n^yU$ a well-defined $H^2$ limit. Let $b=B_{r-1}u$ and $w=u-b$. By [F3], $\|w\|_{H^r(T)}\le B_r|u|_{H^r(T)}$. Set $U=(E_rw)|_{I^2}$ and define $A_{p,r}u=b+(S_n^xS_n^yU)|_T.$ This map is linear. The first summand has degree at most $r-1\le p$; the second lies in $\mathbb Q_n\subseteq\mathbb P_{2n}\subseteq\mathbb P_p$. Since $E_rw=w$ on $T$, step 2.1 and [F2]–[F3] yield $\|u-A_{p,r}u\|_{H^2(T)}\le C M_rB_r\eta_{n,r}|u|_{H^r(T)}.$ This identifies the constant as the absolute tensor constant times the fixed extension and moment bounds; no growth in $r$ is asserted.

Transport step 3.1 to a shape-regular affine triangle $K$. For $e=u-A_{K,p,r}u$ and $\widehat e=e\circ F_K$, two-dimensional affine pullback gives $|\widehat e|_{H^j(T)}\asymp_{j,\gamma}h_K^{j-1}|e|_{H^j(K)}$ for $j=0,1,2$, and $|\widehat u|_{H^r(T)}\le C_{r,\gamma}h_K^{r-1}|u|_{H^r(K)}$ by [F6]. This proves the displayed full scaled estimate. Finally, $\eta_{n,r}^{-2}$ is a product of $2(r-4)$ consecutive integers beginning with $n-r+4$. If $p\ge4(r-2)$ and $n=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$, then $n-r+4\ge p/4$; taking square roots yields $\eta_{n,r}\le(4/p)^{r-4}$.

$$
For $c\in\mathbb R$, define the endpoint-anchored integrated projector
$$
\mathcal I_p(c,g)(x):=c+\int_{-1}^x\Pi_{p-1}g(t)\,dt,\qquad -1\le x\le1.
$$
If an absolutely continuous function $f$ is represented as $f(x)=f(-1)+\int_{-1}^xf'(t)\,dt$ with $f'\in L^2$, write $I_pf:=\mathcal I_p(f(-1),f')$. The finite sum and integral are defined for every such input; no choice axiom is used in this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$, let $T=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0,\ x+y<1\}$, and let $q$ be a real polynomial of degree at most $p$ satisfying $q(0)=q(1)=0$. Define the polynomial $R(t)=q(t)/t$ by cancellation at $t=0$, and put

$$
Lq(x,y)=q(x)-xR(1-y).
$$

Then $Lq\in\mathbb P_p(T)$, it equals $q$ on $y=0$, and it vanishes on $x=0$ and $x+y=1$. Moreover,

$$
\|Lq\|_{H^1(T)}\le4\|q'\|_{L^2(0,1)},
$$

independently of $p$. Permuting the three vertices gives the same bound, up to one fixed constant, for each reference edge. If $K$ is a shape-regular affine triangle, $E$ is an edge of length $\ell_E$, and $h_K=\operatorname{diam}(K)$, the transported lift satisfies

$$
|L_Eq|_{H^1(K)}\le C_\gamma\ell_E^{1/2}\|\partial_\tau q\|_{L^2(E)},\qquad \|L_Eq\|_{L^2(K)}\le C_\gamma h_K\ell_E^{1/2}\|\partial_\tau q\|_{L^2(E)}.

Consequently continuous polynomial data on the three edges of a triangle, each of degree at most the cell degree, have a polynomial extension of that cell degree. The estimate uses the strong $H^1$ edge norm and asserts no optimal $H^{1/2}$ trace-lifting bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0,\ x+y<1\}$, let $r\ge5$ be an integer, let $p\ge2r-4$ be an integer, and put $n=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$ and

$$
\eta_{n,r}=\left(\frac{(n-r+3)!}{(n+r-5)!}\right)^{1/2}.
$$

\|u-A_{p,r}u\|_{H^2(T)}\le C_r\eta_{n,r}|u|_{H^r(T)}.

$$
\left(\sum_{j=0}^2h_K^{2j-2}|u-A_{K,p,r}u|_{H^j(K)}^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_{r,\gamma}\eta_{n,r}h_K^{r-1}|u|_{H^r(K)}.

$1\le p<\infty$, and let
$\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex. Then restrictions of functions

$$|u(x_j)|\le C\|u\|_{W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)}.$$

functional there. No boundedness at $\ell=d/p$ is asserted.

$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$

$$

$$

$$

On every compact subset of $\overline\Omega\setminus\mathcal C$, the derivatives satisfy ordinary factorial bounds $|D^\alpha u|\le C_0A_0^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$. On every closed nondegenerate shape-regular affine triangle $K\subset\overline\Omega$ with $K^\circ\subset\Omega$ and $K\cap\mathcal C=\varnothing$, whose ratio $h_K/\operatorname{dist}(K,\mathcal C)$ is bounded above and below by fixed positive constants, where $\operatorname{dist}(K,\mathcal C)=\inf_{x\in K,c\in\mathcal C}|x-c|$, set $r_K=\min(R,\operatorname{dist}(K,\mathcal C))$. After subtracting a suitable constant from the pullback $\widehat u$ to the reference triangle of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], $\|D^\alpha\widehat u\|_\infty\le C A_1^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!r_K^a$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, with constants uniform over this family. $$

$$

$$

$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let

in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $0<a<\min_i(1-\beta_i)$ as in [F1]. Call a cell a cap when its closure contains a corner. Since the corner set is finite and distinct corners have positive separation, for all sufficiently large $k$ each cap contains at most one corner; its diameter is at most $C_1\sigma^k$. On a noncap cell $T$ with $d_T=\operatorname{dist}(T,\mathcal C)<R$, the mesh condition gives $\sigma\le h_T/d_T\le\sigma^{-1}$, so [F1] gives uniform scaled analytic derivative bounds after subtracting a suitable constant. If $d_T\ge R$, the compact-away-from-corners bounds in [F1], together with bounded $h_T$ and the fixed $r_T=R$, give the same conclusion after enlarging constants. Thus each noncap reference pullback has derivative bounds $C r_T^a A_1^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$, where $r_T=\min(R,d_T)$.

For every mesh edge incident to a polygon corner, prescribe the linear interpolant of the two endpoint values of the continuous representative of $u$. All cells sharing such an edge are caps. On every other edge $E$, prescribe the single common endpoint-preserving derivative-projection polynomial $g_E$ from [F2], in one globally fixed edge orientation. The edge lies a distance comparable to its length from any nearby corner: for an edge opposite a cap corner this follows from shape regularity and the altitude bound, and for a noncap neighbor it also follows from the mesh ratio condition. Thus [F1]–[F2] give, on each noncap edge, $\|u-g_E\|_{L^\infty(E)}+\ell_E^{1/2}\|\partial_\tau(u-g_E)\|_{L^2(E)}\le C r_T^a e^{-bp_k}$ for each adjoining noncap cell, with comparable scales on both sides. Here the sup bound follows from the endpoint identity and $\|e\|_\infty\le\|e'\|_{L^1}\le\|e'\|_{L^2}$ for the endpoint-zero reference error; [F6] justifies the last inequality. On an edge incident to a corner, both adjacent cells are caps, its prescribed linear polynomial shares the exact continuous vertex values, and no tangential regularity of $u$ at the corner is used. Every edge polynomial takes the value of $u$ at both endpoints. If $E\subset\Gamma_D$, these endpoint values and the entire prescribed edge polynomial are zero.

Let $T$ be a noncap triangle and choose $q_T\in\mathbb P_{p_k}(T)$ by transporting the analytic approximation [F2] for the scaled pullback, then adding back its subtracted constant. Thus $\|u-q_T\|_\infty+h_T\|\nabla(u-q_T)\|_\infty\le Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}$. Correct its three vertex values by an affine polynomial to obtain $\widetilde q_T$ matching the prescribed $g_E$ at all vertices; the correction has $H^1$ seminorm at most $Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}$. On each edge, $g_E-\widetilde q_T|_E$ has zero endpoints, degree at most $p_k$, and strong edge derivative norm at most $Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}$. Lift these three residuals separately by [F3]. Their sum does not change the other edge traces, so the resulting $v_T\in\mathbb P_{p_k}(T)$ has all three prescribed traces and $|u-v_T|_{H^1(T)}\le Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}\le Ce^{-bp_k}.$

Let $T$ be a cap at corner $c_i$, with diameter $h_T$; for large $k$ it contains no other corner. Start with the affine interpolant $a_T$ of the three exact vertex values. By [F1], $|u-a_T|_{H^1(T)}\le Ch_T^a$. Its two edges incident to $c_i$ already have the prescribed linear traces. On the opposite edge $E$, every point has distance comparable to $h_T$ from $c_i$, so the gradient bound in [F1] and Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] give $\ell_E^{1/2}\|\partial_\tau u\|_{L^2(E)}\le Ch_T^a$. The interval derivative projection in [F2] is contractive, and the vertex estimate in [F1] gives the same bound for $g_E-a_T|_E$. This discrepancy vanishes at both endpoints; add its lift from [F3]. The resulting polynomial has all prescribed traces and $|u-v_T|_{H^1(T)}\le Ch_T^a\le C\sigma^{ak}$. No $H^2$ regularity is used on a cap.
